Replace 'work' from their probe answer with trabajo, then practise short phrases such as mi trabajo, la reunión and el proyecto.","key_facts":["El = the (masculine singular); la = the (feminine singular).","Los and las = the (plural).","Un = a (masculine); una = a (feminine).","Many nouns ending in -o are masculine and many ending in -a are feminine, but there are exceptions.","El trabajo = the work or job; el proyecto = the project; el correo = the email.","La reunión = the meeting; la oficina = the office; la empresa = the company.","El problema and el día are masculine despite ending in -a.","Add -s after a vowel and -es after most consonants: proyectos, reuniones."],"misconceptions":["Copying a noun's gender from Hindi or Gujarati.","Assuming every noun ending in -a is feminine.","Mixing English nouns into Spanish, as in 'Mi work'."]},{"id":"ar-verbs-work","title":"Talking About Work with -ar Verbs","objective":"Say what you do at work and form simple negative sentences with common -ar verbs.","teach_notes":"Fix 'Mi work estu' by offering Trabajo en... and Mi trabajo es... Drill true sentences about their job, then negate them by placing no before the verb. Contrast estar with ser using simple labels: estar for current condition and location, ser for identity. Since Hindi 'है' covers both, use many paired examples. Practise real work check-ins, such as answering how they are and whether they are busy.","key_facts":["Estoy = I am; estás = you are (tú); está = he or she is, or you are (usted).","Estamos = we are; están = they are, or you all are.","Estoy bien = I am well; never 'Soy bien' for this meaning.","Estoy ocupado or estoy ocupada = I am busy.","Estoy en la oficina = I am in the office.","¿Dónde está el informe? = Where is the report?","Use ser for identity: Soy Alex.","Use estar for temporary conditions and for location: Estoy cansado, estoy en casa."],"misconceptions":["Inventing forms like 'estu' instead of estoy or está.","Saying 'Soy en la oficina' for location.","Thinking estar is only for temporary things; location of people and objects also uses estar."]},{"id":"time-today-tomorrow","title":"Hoy, Mañana and Meeting Times","objective":"Talk about today, tomorrow, weekdays and meeting times without confusion.","teach_notes":"Fix the probe error first: mañana does not mean today. Then show that mañana also means morning, using mañana por la mañana. Finish with scheduling sentences about real meetings, including days and clock times.","key_facts":["Hoy = today; ayer = yesterday; mañana = tomorrow.","La mañana = the morning; por la mañana = in the morning.","Mañana por la mañana = tomorrow morning.","Days: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo (lowercase).","El lunes = on Monday; los lunes = on Mondays.","Es la una = It is one o'clock; son las tres = It is three o'clock.","La reunión es a las tres = The meeting is at three.","¿A qué hora es la reunión? = What time is the meeting?"],"misconceptions":["Thinking mañana means today.","Adding en before weekdays, as in 'en lunes', instead of el lunes.","Saying 'son las una' instead of es la una."]},{"id":"asking-questions","title":"Asking Questions at Work","objective":"Ask for key information about people, tasks, places and times.","teach_notes":"Teach question words as tools for real work tasks. (usted).","Más despacio, por favor = More slowly, please.","¿Cómo se dice 'deadline' en español? = How do you say 'deadline' in Spanish?","Gracias = thank you; de nada = you're welcome.","Hasta mañana = See you tomorrow; nos vemos = see you.","In Peru, ya often means OK or got it in conversation.","Chévere = great or cool, in casual speech; ahorita = right now or soon, and can be imprecise."],"misconceptions":["Staying silent or pretending to understand rather than using a repair phrase.","Taking ahorita as a precise time commitment.","Using casual words like chévere in a formal client setting before gauging the tone."]}]}

{"explain":"Spanish vowels are short and steady, like Hindi/English but more pure. H is always silent (hola = 'ola). The single r is a quick tap like Hindi र. J sounds like Hindi ह but rougher (trabajo). Ñ is like 'ny' in canyon, close to Hindi ञ (mañana). In Peru, z and c before e/i sound like s: cinco, gracias. Example: say 'hola' as 'ola', 'pero' with a quick tap r like 'pe-ro', and 'mañana' with 'ny' sound like 'ma-nya-no'.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"How should 'hola' be pronounced?","options":["HO-la with strong H like Hindi ह","O-la with silent H","HO-lah with aspirated H like English",'O-lah with H barely audible'],"answer":"O-la with silent H","why":"In Spanish, H is always silent, so hola sounds like 'ola'."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does the Spanish single r sound like?","options":["Trilled like English r in run","A quick tap like Hindi र","A guttural sound like French r",'A soft buzz like Japanese っ'],"answer":"A quick tap like Hindi र","why":"A single r in Spanish is a quick tap, similar to the Hindi र sound."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sounds like the Spanish ñ in 'mañana'?","options":["Hindi त","Hindi ञ (like 'ny' in canyon)","Hindi न",'Hindi ह'],"answer":"Hindi ञ (like 'ny' in canyon)","why":"Spanish ñ is pronounced like 'ny' in canyon, close to Hindi ञ."},{"type":"mcq","q":"In Peruvian Spanish, how does 'cinco' sound?","options":["sin-co (z like s)","kin-co (z like k)","tsin-co (z like 'ts')",'sin-kho (z aspirated)'],"answer":"sin-co (z like s)","why":"In Peru, z and c before e/i sound like s, so cinco is pronounced 'sin-co'."},{"type":"recall","q":"Spell the Spanish greeting used in the morning.","answer":"Buenos días","why":"'Buenos días' is used for morning greetings."},{"type":"recall","q":"Spell the Spanish greeting used in the evening or night.","answer":"Buenas noches","why":"'Buenas noches' is used for evening and night greetings."}]}

{"explain":"Spanish vowels are short and pure: a, e, i, o, u sound like आ, ए, ई, ओ, ऊ, but never glide. Take trabajo (work): tra-BA-jo. The j is a strong English h, and the stress falls on BA because the word ends in a vowel. H is silent, so hola sounds like 'OH-la'. Ñ is the ny in 'canyon', so mañana is 'ma-NYA-na'. In Peru, ll sounds like English y, so me llamo is 'me YA-mo'. Words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the second-to-last syllable. A written accent marks an exception, as in reunión. Say each word aloud and keep your vowels steady.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"How is the h in hola pronounced?","options":["It is silent, so it sounds like 'ola'","It is a breathy English h, as in 'hat'","It is a hard k sound, as in 'kite'","It is an English s sound, as in 'sun'"],"answer":"It is silent, so it sounds like 'ola'","why":"Spanish h is always silent, so hola is read as 'OH-la'."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sound does ñ make in mañana?","options":["The ny sound in 'canyon'","The plain n sound in 'name'","The ng sound in 'sing'","The k sound in 'kitchen'"],"answer":"The ny sound in 'canyon'","why":"Ñ is a separate letter that sounds like the ny in 'canyon', so mañana is 'ma-NYA-na'."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Where is the stress in trabajo?","options":["On the first syllable: TRA-ba-jo","On the second syllable: tra-BA-jo","On the last syllable: tra-ba-JO","Evenly across all syllables"],"answer":"On the second syllable: tra-BA-jo","why":"Trabajo ends in a vowel, so the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable, BA."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How does the ll in me llamo sound in Peru?","options":["Like the English y in 'yes'","Like the English l in 'lamp'","Like the English j in 'jam'","Like the English k in 'kite'"],"answer":"Like the English y in 'yes'","why":"In Peru, ll usually sounds like English y, so llamo is 'YA-mo'."},{"type":"recall","q":"Read trabajo aloud, then say which sound the j makes and where the stress falls.","answer":"The j is a strong English h, so it is tra-BA-ho, with stress on BA.","why":"Spanish j is a strong h, and the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable of a vowel-ending word."},{"type":"recall","q":"Read mañana aloud and explain the sound of ñ and where the stress falls.","answer":"ma-NYA-na: ñ sounds like the ny in 'canyon', and the stress falls on NYA because the word ends in a vowel.","why":"Mañana means tomorrow, not today, so practising its sound now helps you use it correctly at work."}]}

{"explain":"To say your name, use 'Me llamo' (literally 'I call myself') or 'Mi nombre es' ('My name is', just like 'Mera naam hai' in Hindi). Never mix them into 'mi llamo' or 'me nombre'. Note that 'mi' means 'my' and stays lowercase mid-sentence. To ask a coworker's name informally, say '¿Cómo te llamas?'; for a client formally, ask '¿Cómo se llama?'. When introduced, say 'Mucho gusto' (Nice to meet you) and reply with 'Igualmente' (Likewise). For example: 'Hola, me llamo Alex. ¿Cómo te llamas?'","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which phrase correctly states your name in Spanish?","options":["Me llamo Alex.","Mi llamo Alex.","Me nombre es Alex.","Yo nombre Alex."],"answer":"Me llamo Alex.","why":"'Me llamo' literally means 'I call myself' and is never combined with 'mi'."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which question should you ask to find out a Peruvian client contact's name formally?","options":["¿Cómo se llama?","¿Cómo te llamas?","¿Cómo te llamo?","¿Cómo se nombre?"],"answer":"¿Cómo se llama?","why":"'¿Cómo se llama?' is the formal way to ask someone's name in Spanish."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How should you politely reply to someone who just said 'Mucho gusto' to you?","options":["Igualmente","Me llamo","Mucho nombre","Cómo se llama"],"answer":"Igualmente","why":"'Igualmente' means 'Likewise' and is the standard polite reply to 'Mucho gusto'."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which sentence follows correct Spanish capitalization rules mid-sentence?","options":["Hola, me llamo Juan y mi nombre es corto.","Hola, me llamo Juan y Mi nombre es corto.","Hola, mi llamo Juan y Mi nombre es corto.","Hola, me nombre Juan y mi llamo corto."],"answer":"Hola, me llamo Juan y mi nombre es corto.","why":"Words like 'mi' must stay lowercase when they appear in the middle of a sentence."},{"type":"recall","q":"Translate 'My name is Alex' using the pattern that matches 'Mera naam hai'.","answer":"Mi nombre es Alex.","why":"'Mi nombre es' translates word-for-word to 'My name is', matching the Hindi structure."},{"type":"recall","q":"What Spanish phrase means 'Nice to meet you' when meeting a coworker?","answer":"Mucho gusto","why":"'Mucho gusto' is the standard polite expression meaning 'Nice to meet you'."}]}

{"explain":"Use \"me llamo\" to say your name: Me llamo Alex. Literally it means \"I call myself Alex,\" so \"me\" is not \"my.\" \"Mi\" means \"my\" and goes before a noun, as in mi nombre es Alex (my name is Alex). So say Me llamo, never Mi llamo. To ask someone's name, use ¿Cómo te llamas? with a friend or coworker you know well, or ¿Cómo se llama? with someone formal, such as a client. Reply with Mucho gusto (nice to meet you). Use 'usted' (like 'aap' or 'tame') for one client or senior colleague to show polite respect. When greeting a client, ask '¿Cómo está usted?' instead of '¿Cómo estás?'. For any group of people ('you all'), always use 'ustedes' in Peru. Also, Spanish speakers often drop these words entirely because the verb already makes the person clear. Start with 'usted' for clients until invited to use 'tú'.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which word for 'you' should you use when greeting an important new client individually?","options":["usted","tú","ustedes","él"],"answer":"usted","why":"Usted is the polite, formal singular form of 'you' used with clients and seniors."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which pronoun matches the informal 'you' used with a familiar coworker, similar to Hindi 'tum'?","options":["tú","usted","ustedes","nosotros"],"answer":"tú","why":"Tú is the informal singular 'you' reserved for friends and close peers."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When addressing a team of Peruvian coworkers together as a group, which pronoun means 'you all'?","options":["ustedes","usted","tú","ellos"],"answer":"ustedes","why":"Ustedes is the plural form of 'you' used for groups in Peru."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How should you formally ask a senior client 'How are you?' in a meeting?","options":["¿Cómo está?","¿Cómo estás?","¿Cómo soy?","¿Cómo eres?"],"answer":"¿Cómo está?","why":"¿Cómo está? is the formal singular phrasing paired with usted."},{"type":"recall","q":"Which single Spanish pronoun means formal 'you' (singular) for addressing a client respectfully?","answer":"usted","why":"Usted provides the respectful singular address equivalent to 'aap'."},{"type":"recall","q":"In Peru, which Spanish word is used to address two or more people as 'you all'?","answer":"ustedes","why":"Ustedes is the standard plural 'you' across Latin America."}]}

{"learner":"Level: strong in Python (classes, dicts, asyncio), but new to Rust and compiled languages.\nGoal: go from zero to building, testing, and shipping production Rust.\nKnown gaps: compilation and static types; shaky confidence in move semantics; has never seen a borrow checker.","nodes":[{"id":"cargo-and-basics","title":"Cargo, Compilation, and Basic Syntax","objective":"Create and run a Cargo project, write simple typed functions, and read basic compiler errors.","teach_notes":"Contrast Python, which surfaces many errors at runtime, with Rust, which rejects many before the program runs. Keep this practical and leave advanced lifetimes for later.","key_facts":["String owns growable UTF-8 text.","&str is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text.","String literals have the type &'static str.","Prefer &str over &String for read-only string parameters.","Rust strings cannot be indexed by integer, so s[0] does not compile.","String slice ranges use byte offsets and panic if they do not fall on character boundaries.","&[T] is a borrowed view of contiguous elements.","Lifetime annotations describe relationships between references and do not change how long values live."],"misconceptions":["Slicing creates a separate copy, as it does with a Python list.","Adding a lifetime annotation makes data live longer.","String length counts characters rather than bytes."]},{"id":"structs-enums-match","title":"Structs, Enums, and Pattern Matching","objective":"Model data with structs and enums, add methods, and handle variants with match.","teach_notes":"Map their classes to struct plus impl, while separating data from behavior. Explain panics as closer to unrecoverable bugs than ordinary exceptions. Recommend a simple rule: thiserror for libraries, anyhow for applications. Warn against scattering unwrap through production code.","key_facts":["Result<T, E> has two variants: Ok(T) and Err(E).","The ? operator returns early with the error if a Result is Err, and otherwise yields the Ok value.","? converts the error type using the From trait where a suitable conversion exists.","? can be used only in a function whose return type supports it, such as Result or Option.","unwrap() panics on Err or None.","expect(\"message\") also panics, but includes the given message.","panic! is intended for unrecoverable errors and bugs.","thiserror is commonly used for defining library error types, and anyhow for application-level error handling."],"misconceptions":["panic! is Rust's equivalent of raising an ordinary exception; expected failures should use Result.","? swallows or ignores an error; it propagates the error to the caller.","unwrap() is harmless in production because a value usually exists; it crashes the thread when that assumption fails."]},{"id":"strings-slices-lifetimes","title":"Strings, Slices and Lifetimes","objective":"Choose between String and &str, use slices safely, and read and write basic lifetime annotations.","teach_notes":"Python has one str type, so explain the split through ownership: String owns its text, while &str borrows a view of it. Show iter versus into_iter using their ownership knowledge. Finish with one trait implemented on a struct, and one generic function with a bound, keeping dyn brief.","key_facts":["Vec<T> is a growable array whose elements all have type T.","HashMap::get returns an Option containing a reference to the value, not a value that can raise KeyError.","A trait defines shared behavior that types implement using impl Trait for Type.","fn show<T: Display>(x: T) is a generic function with a trait bound.","Generics are usually monomorphized, producing specialized code for each concrete type at compile time.","dyn Trait uses dynamic dispatch at runtime.","Iterator adapters such as map and filter are lazy and do nothing until consumed, for example by collect.","iter() yields shared references, iter_mut() yields mutable references, and into_iter() on an owned collection yields owned values."],"misconceptions":["Calling map on an iterator runs immediately; it does nothing until the iterator is consumed.","Traits are the same as base classes; they define behavior but have no instance fields or class inheritance.","for x in vec leaves vec usable as Python would; this consumes the Vec, so use &vec to borrow it."]},{"id":"shared-state-and-async","title":"Shared State and Async with Tokio","objective":"Share state safely between tasks using Arc and Mutex, and write concurrent async code with Tokio.","teach_notes":"Build on asyncio: async, await and tasks will look familiar, but Rust has no built-in runtime, so Tokio supplies one. {"explain":"In Python, b = a gives two names for one list. Rust works differently: each value has exactly one owner. Take let a = vec![1, 2, 3]; let b = a; Ownership moves to b, and using a afterward is a compile error. Passing a Vec into a function by value moves it the same way. When the owner goes out of scope, Rust drops the value and frees it, with no garbage collector. Copy types like i32, f64, bool, and char are duplicated on assignment instead. clone() makes an explicit copy, and its cost depends on the type.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"After let b = a; where a is a Vec, what happens to a?","options":["It is moved, so using it is a compile error","It still works and shares its data with b","It is copied automatically, so both are usable","It is reset to an empty Vec"],"answer":"It is moved, so using it is a compile error","why":"Assigning a non-Copy value like Vec transfers ownership, so a can no longer be used."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which of these is a Copy type?","options":["String","Vec<char>","bool","Vec<f64>"],"answer":"bool","why":"bool is a Copy type, so it is duplicated on assignment, while String and Vec<T> are not Copy."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When is a value dropped in Rust?","options":["When its owner goes out of scope","When the garbage collector runs","When its reference count reaches zero","When the program ends"],"answer":"When its owner goes out of scope","why":"Rust has one owner per value and drops the value when that owner goes out of scope, with no garbage collector or reference counting by default."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens when you pass a Vec to a function by value?","options":["It moves into the function, and the caller can no longer use it","It is cloned automatically, and the caller keeps its copy","It is shared, and both sides can still read it","It stays with the caller, and the function gets a second name for it"],"answer":"It moves into the function, and the caller can no longer use it","why":"Passing a non-Copy value by value transfers ownership, the same as assignment does."},{"type":"recall","q":"Why can Rust free a value without a garbage collector?","answer":"Each value has exactly one owner, so when that owner goes out of scope Rust drops the value at that point, deterministically.","why":"Single ownership makes the drop point known at compile time, so no runtime collector or reference counting is needed."},{"type":"recall","q":"Given let v = vec![1, 2, 3]; let w = v; what happens if you use v afterward, and how can you keep both usable?","answer":"Using v is a compile error because it was moved to w. Writing let w = v.clone(); gives w its own duplicate, so both stay usable, at the cost of copying the heap data.","why":"A move transfers ownership, and clone() is the explicit way to duplicate a value when you need both."}]}

{"explain":"In Python, you can change a list while looping over it, and that often causes bugs. Rust catches this kind of problem at compile time with the borrow checker. A reference is a borrow. &T is shared and read-only, and many can exist at once. &mut T is mutable, and while it exists, no other reference to that value can exist. Creating &mut x requires x to be declared with mut. A borrow ends after its last use, not at the closing brace. Example: let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3]; let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!(\"{}\", first); fails to compile. push may reallocate the vector, which would leave first pointing at freed memory. Fix it by finishing with first before calling push. Borrow checking adds no runtime cost.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which set of borrows can exist at the same time for one value?","options":["Many shared &T references and no mutable reference","Two &mut T references at once","One &mut T alongside a &T","Several &T references plus one &mut T"],"answer":"Many shared &T references and no mutable reference","why":"The rule is many shared readers or one writer, never both at once."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does the code let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!(\"{}\", first); fail to compile?","options":["Vec::push may reallocate and move the element first points to","The index 0 cannot be used to borrow from a Vec","first is not declared with let mut","push returns a value that is never used"],"answer":"Vec::push may reallocate and move the element first points to","why":"Pushing can reallocate the buffer, so the shared reference to an element would dangle while it is still used."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What must be true before you can create &mut x?","options":["x must be declared with mut","x must be a Vec","x must already be borrowed once","x must be passed into a function"],"answer":"x must be declared with mut","why":"A mutable reference requires the underlying variable to be declared mutable."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When does a borrow end?","options":["After its last use","At the closing brace of its scope","When the enclosing function returns","When the program exits"],"answer":"After its last use","why":"The borrow checker ends a borrow after its final use, so the scope's end is not the cutoff."},{"type":"recall","q":"What does passing &value to a function let the function do, and what does it not do?","answer":"It lets the function use the value without taking ownership; the caller keeps the value and can still use it afterward.","why":"Passing a reference borrows the value instead of moving it, so ownership stays with the caller."},{"type":"recall","q":"In the Vec push error, how do you fix it while keeping the same logic?","answer":"Narrow or reorder the borrow: finish using the element reference before calling push, so the shared borrow ends before the mutable use.","why":"Once the shared borrow's last use is done, the mutable push no longer conflicts with it."}]}

{"explain":"In Python, `b = a` points two names to the same object. Rust does not have a garbage collector, so it enforces a strict rule: every value has exactly one owner, and when that owner exits its scope, Rust drops the value immediately.

For non-`Copy` types like `String`, assignment or passing by value transfers ownership—this is a move. For example:
```rust
let a = String::from("hello");
let b = a; // `a` is moved to `b`; `a` is now invalid
```
Heap data is not copied during a move; only ownership shifts. To preserve `a`, call `a.clone()` explicitly. In contrast, primitive stack types like `i32` implement `Copy`, copying bitwise on assignment without invalidating the source.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens to variable `a` after executing `let a = String::from("service"); let b = a;` in Rust?","options":["`a` is invalidated at compile time because ownership was moved to `b`.","`a` and `b` share the same heap data via automatic reference counting.","`a` remains valid because the heap buffer is deep-copied automatically into `b`.","`a` is marked as a null reference until re-initialized by the program runtime."],"answer":"`a` is invalidated at compile time because ownership was moved to `b`.","why":"Assigning a `String` moves ownership to the new variable, rendering the original variable unusable."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does Rust mandate that every non-`Copy` value has exactly one owner at any given moment?","options":["To prevent heap fragmentation across concurrent runtime threads.","To enforce a predictable single point for dropping memory without a garbage collector.","To allow the compiler to inline every heap allocation into stack frames directly.","To restrict data mutations to single-threaded routines within the same module scope."],"answer":"To enforce a predictable single point for dropping memory without a garbage collector.","why":"Having exactly one owner guarantees that heap memory is deallocated once and only once when that owner exits scope."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which behavior occurs when assigning `let y = x;` where `x` is a value of type `i32`?","options":["`x` is invalidated immediately because primitive integers are always moved.","`x` transfers ownership to `y` and cannot be read unless cloned explicitly.","`x` remains completely valid because `i32` implements the `Copy` trait.","`y` becomes an immutable pointer to the stack memory cell of `x`."],"answer":"`x` remains completely valid because `i32` implements the `Copy` trait.","why":"Primitive integers implement `Copy`, meaning values are bitwise duplicated upon assignment rather than moved."},{"type":"mcq","q":"If you must keep a `String` variable `s` usable after passing it to a function `process(s)`, what explicit method call creates an independent duplicate?","options":["`s.clone()`","`s.copy()`","`s.retain()`","`s.fork()`"],"answer":"`s.clone()`","why":"`clone()` explicitly creates a duplicate of heap data so the original value can remain owned."},{"type":"recall","q":"When a non-`Copy` value such as a `String` is passed directly by value into a function parameter, what happens to the caller's variable?","answer":"Ownership moves into the function, making the caller's variable invalid and unusable.","why":"Passing a non-`Copy` value by value transfers ownership to the callee, invalidating the original caller variable."},{"type":"recall","q":"What happens to heap-allocated memory managed by a `String` owner when that owner's variable exits its enclosing {"explain":"In Rust, each value has exactly one owner. When you assign a non-Copy type like String to another variable, ownership moves—the original binding becomes unusable. For example, `let s1 = String::from(\"hello\"); let s2 = s1; println!(\"{}\", s1);` fails to compile because `s1` no longer owns its value after the move to `s2`. This differs from Python where `b = a` creates two references to the same object. Copy types like i32 are duplicated implicitly, while heap-owning types require explicit `.clone()` to duplicate.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens to the original binding `s1` after executing `let s1 = String::from(\"test\"); let s2 = s1;`?","options":["s1 is still usable and holds \"test\"","s1 becomes unusable (moved)","s1 is automatically cloned","s1 is set to null"],"answer":"s1 becomes unusable (moved)","why":"Assigning a non-Copy type like String transfers ownership, leaving the original binding invalid."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which of these types is moved by default when assigned to another variable?","options":["i32","bool","String","char"],"answer":"String","why":"String owns heap data and is not a Copy type, so assignment moves ownership."},{"type":"mcq","q":"How do you explicitly create a duplicate of a String value in Rust?","options":["s.clone()","s.copy()","s.dup()","&s"],"answer":"s.clone()","why":"clone() is the explicit method to create a deep copy of heap-owning data."},{"type":"mcq","q":"When does Rust automatically free a value's memory?","options":["When the programmer calls drop() explicitly","When the owner goes out of scope","When the function returns","When the program exits"],"answer":"When the owner goes out of scope","why":"Ownership rules guarantee deterministic cleanup via the drop method when the owner leaves scope."},{"type":"recall","q":"Name two Rust types that are Copy types (automatically duplicated on assignment).","answer":"i32 and bool","why":"i32, f64, bool, and char are primitive Copy types that duplicate on assignment rather than move."},{"type":"recall","q":"What is the core difference between Python's `b = a` and Rust's `let b = a` when a is a String?","answer":"Python creates two references to one object; Rust transfers ownership so a becomes unusable.","why":"This captures the fundamental distinction: reference sharing vs. single ownership transfer."}]}

{"explain":"Start with what you know: hola means hello. Greet people by time of day: Buenos días (good morning, until about noon), Buenas tardes (good afternoon), and Buenas noches (good evening, or goodnight). Don't use buenas noches as a daytime hello. To ask how someone is, use ¿Cómo estás? with a friend, since it's informal with tú. With a client or senior, use the formal ¿Cómo está usted? Like Hindi and Gujarati, Spanish separates informal and formal address. Reply with Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? (or ¿Y usted? to a client). When you meet someone, say Mucho gusto (Nice to meet you). Example at 9 a.m. with a client: Buenos días. ¿Cómo está usted?","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which greeting fits when you meet a coworker at 8 p.m.?","options":["Buenos días","Buenas tardes","Buenas noches","Buenas mañanas"],"answer":"Buenas noches","why":"Buenas noches is the greeting for the evening, while buenos días is for the morning."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which question is the formal way to ask a client how they are?","options":["¿Cómo estás?","¿Cómo está usted?","¿Cómo estamos?","¿Cómo eres?"],"answer":"¿Cómo está usted?","why":"Usted is the formal address used with clients and superiors, so the question uses está usted."},{"type":"mcq","q":"What does Mucho gusto mean?","options":["Nice to meet you","Good morning","How are you?","Thank you very much"],"answer":"Nice to meet you","why":"Mucho gusto is said when you are introduced to someone for the first time."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which greeting fits at 11 a.m.?","options":["Buenos días","Buenas tardes","Buenas noches","Mucho gusto"],"answer":"Buenos días","why":"Buenos días is used until about noon, so 11 a.m. is still morning."},{"type":"recall","q":"It is 10 a.m. You are greeting a client formally and asking how they are. {"explain":"Spanish has five vowels: a, e, i, o, u. Each has one pure sound and never glides as English vowels do, so a is 'ah', never 'ay'. The h is silent, so hola sounds like 'OH-la'. The j is a throaty sound like the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch', as in jamón. The ñ sounds like 'ny' in 'canyon'. A single r is a quick tap, while rr is a rolled trill: pero (but) vs. perro (dog). For stress, words ending in a vowel, n or s put the stress on the second-to-last syllable: tra-BA-jo. Words that break this rule get a written accent: teléfono, está.","items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"How is hola pronounced?","options":["OH-la","HO-la","OH-lay","HOH-la"],"answer":"OH-la","why":"The h is silent, so the word begins with the vowel sound."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which pair shows the difference between a single tap r and a rolled rr?","options":["pero / perro","hola / ola","mano / mono","gato / gado"],"answer":"pero / perro","why":"Pero (but) has a single tap r, while perro (dog) has a rolled rr."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Where is the stress in trabajo?","options":["TRA-ba-jo","tra-BA-jo","tra-ba-JO","tra-ba-jo (even)"],"answer":"tra-BA-jo","why":"Trabajo ends in a vowel, so the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable, ba."},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which is the correct sound for the Spanish vowel a?","options":["ah","ay","eh-ee","uh"],"answer":"ah","why":"Spanish vowels are pure and do not glide, so a is always 'ah'."},{"type":"recall","q":"What sound does ñ make, and which English word has the same sound?","answer":"It sounds like 'ny', as in 'canyon'.","why":"ñ is the 'ny' sound, which English shows in 'canyon'."},{"type":"recall","q":"Using the stress rule, where is the stress in tra-ba-jo, and why?","answer":"On the second-to-last syllable, tra-BA-jo, because the word ends in a vowel.","why":"Words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the second-to-last syllable."}]}
